buildUp: Start with the graphics you want, which sets how much computing you need, and put the processor and graphics on one custom chip so they can share memory and cost less than separate parts.
Feed that chip with very fast graphics memory placed right around it, and with solid-state storage quick enough that games load in seconds.
The chip runs at about 1 volt but draws around 200 watts, so the main board must deliver over 100 amps cleanly, and a built-in power supply converts mains electricity down to safe low voltages.
All 200 watts becomes heat, so a thin liquid-metal layer pulls it out of the chip, heat pipes spread it across a large finned heat sink, and a big, slow fan blows air through.
The box must sit in a living room, so the airflow path is planned from the vents through the heat sink and out the back, and the shell is shaped around it.
Finally the things you plug into a TV: HDMI for 4K pictures, USB ports for controllers, a slot to add storage, and a disc drive for Blu-ray games and films.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Design one fixed machine around one custom chip that holds both the processor and the graphics, sharing a single pool of fast memory, and build exactly the same box millions of times. Because every console is identical, game developers can tune for it precisely, and because the whole box is designed together, a big, slow fan and a large heat sink can carry the heat away quietly.

hardParts.title: Removing 200 watts quietly
hardParts.why: The heat has to leave a chip about the size of a postage stamp, spread across a heat sink many times bigger, and be carried off by air, all without the fan becoming noticeable from the sofa. Every part of the path, from fin spacing to vent shape, has to be tuned together, and it has to keep working when the room is warm or dust builds up.

hardParts.title: Getting heat out of the chip itself
hardParts.why: The first fraction of a millimetre, between chip and cooler, is a bottleneck, because ordinary paste conducts heat poorly. Liquid metal conducts several times better, but it also conducts electricity and can corrode some metals, so it has to be sealed in perfectly for years in a box that gets carried around and tipped on its side.

hardParts.title: Feeding a hungry chip
hardParts.why: The chip needs over 100 amps at about 1 volt, delivered steadily even as its demand jumps thousands of times a second, and it needs hundreds of gigabytes of data a second from memory. That means a many-layered board with short, carefully matched wiring, because at these speeds even a few millimetres of extra track can spoil a signal.

principles.explanation: Every pixel needs the same kind of lighting and colour sum, so the graphics part of the chip has thousands of small, simple cores that all do the same calculation on different pixels at once. A 4K picture has about 8.3 million pixels, and at 60 frames a second that's about 500 million pixels every second, each needing its own lighting and colour worked out. The cores share them out like a whole classroom each colouring one square of a mosaic. At roughly 10 teraflops, it can do about 20,000 calculations per pixel in every frame.
principles.title: Graphics is the same sum done millions of times

principles.explanation: A processor is only as fast as the data you can feed it, so the console gives its processor and graphics one shared pool of fast memory delivering roughly 448 gigabytes a second. Eight memory chips, each with 32 data connections running at about 14 gigabits a second, give 256 lanes and that 448 gigabytes a second in total. Sharing that one pool between processor and graphics means data doesn't have to be copied from one to the other, which in a PC is a common bottleneck.
principles.title: Fast chips starve without fast memory

principles.explanation: A chip doesn't use up electricity, it turns it all into heat, so a console playing a game is a 200-watt heater. Solid metal conducts that heat too slowly to spread it across a big heat sink, so heat pipes do it instead: a little liquid inside boils at the hot end, the vapour rushes to the cool end and condenses, then flows back through a wick. Carrying heat as evaporation, like sweat cooling your skin, moves it many times faster than solid copper could.
principles.title: Every watt becomes heat

principles.explanation: Fan noise rises very steeply with blade speed, so the console moves its cooling air with a big fan spinning slowly rather than a small one spinning fast. To remove heat you need to move a certain amount of air, but doubling a fan's speed makes it roughly 15 decibels louder, which sounds about three times as loud. That's why the console uses a fan about 120 mm across and 45 mm thick and a large finned heat sink: plenty of air moves, but slowly enough to stay quiet.
principles.title: Big fans are quiet fans

firstPrinciples.problem: Put lifelike, smooth 3D graphics on a living-room TV, for a price millions of families will pay, in a box that's quiet enough to forget about and keeps working for years. A gaming PC can do the graphics, but it's built from separate expensive parts and often sounds like a hairdryer; the chips doing the work turn around 200 watts into heat that has to go somewhere.

questions.answer: Almost all of it becomes heat in your room, apart from a tiny amount of light and sound. The console is, in effect, a small electric heater that happens to make pictures along the way.
questions.question: Where do the roughly 200 watts the console draws while gaming end up?

questions.answer: Both can move the same amount of air, but noise rises very steeply with fan speed. A larger fan spinning slowly moves plenty of air while staying much quieter.
questions.question: Why use one big slow fan instead of a small fast one?

questions.answer: So data doesn't have to be copied between separate memories, which takes time. Both can work on the same textures and game data directly, and it's cheaper than fitting two sets of memory.
questions.question: Why do the processor and graphics share one pool of memory?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The real advantage is that every console is the same. A PC game has to work on thousands of combinations of parts, but a console game is written for exactly one, so developers can squeeze out performance a PC with similar specifications often can't match. Building tens of millions of identical units also makes a custom chip and a custom cooling system affordable, which no single PC part maker could justify.

name: Game Console
overview:
A games console is a gaming PC designed as a single appliance. Instead of separate parts from different makers, almost everything is built around one custom chip, an APU, that combines an eight-core processor with a powerful graphics unit. Around it on the main board sit fast graphics memory shared by both, and solid-state storage quick enough that games load in seconds rather than minutes.

Because every console is identical, game developers can tune their games to squeeze the most out of exactly this hardware, which is why a console often punches above what a PC with similar specifications can do.

Much of the box is about heat and power. The chip can draw around 200 watts while playing, so it sits under a large metal heat sink with copper heat pipes, and a big, slow fan pulls air through the case to keep it quiet. The power supply is built in, converting mains electricity to the low voltages the chips need, and a disc drive reads Blu-ray discs for games and films.

parts.description: Clip-on plastic panel over the top; it pops off to reach the storage expansion slot and dust catchers.

details.didYouKnow: Because the covers simply clip on, many consoles of this kind can be given a new colour just by swapping the panels, with no tools and no effect on the warranty.
details.howItWorks: The top cover is mostly cosmetic: it hangs on hooks along its edges and slides off without tools, so there are no screws to lose. Underneath it sit the storage expansion slot behind a small screwed plate and the dust catchers, little holes where dust that collects in the air path can be sucked out with a vacuum cleaner. Gaps along its edges line up with the chassis vents so air can flow in and out.
keyNumbers: Console roughly 36 x 8 x 22 cm lying flat
Whole console about 3 kg
Covers typically a few millimetres thick
details.madeOf: Injection-moulded plastic such as ABS or polycarbonate, often with a matt or textured finish. Plastic is cheap to mould into large curved shapes, light, and does not block the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth signals from the antennas inside.

parts.name: Top cover

parts.description: Plastic panel underneath with vents that let cool air in.

details.didYouKnow: Almost every watt a console draws from the wall ends up as heat in your room, so a long gaming session warms a small room about as much as a couple of old-style 100 W light bulbs left on.
details.howItWorks: The bottom cover mirrors the top one and clips onto the chassis in the same way. Its vents and edge gaps let cool room air reach the fan, which is why the console needs some space around it and should not sit on a soft surface like carpet that can block the openings. Small feet or a stand keep it lifted off the surface whether it lies flat or stands upright.
keyNumbers: Typically several centimetres of clearance recommended around vents
Whole console about 3 kg
Gaming draws roughly 200 W, all of which ends up as heat to remove
details.madeOf: Injection-moulded plastic matching the top cover. Plastic keeps the outside cool to the touch and is easy to mould with vent slots and clip hooks in one piece.

parts.name: Bottom cover

parts.description: Metal frame and side walls that everything screws into, with vents at the front and back.

details.didYouKnow: Home consoles have grown a lot in size over the decades, mainly because chips that draw around 200 W need far bigger coolers than the few-watt chips in 1980s machines.
details.howItWorks: The chassis is the console's skeleton: the main board, power supply, disc drive, fan and heat sink are all screwed to it, and the plastic covers hang off its outside. It holds the heavy heat sink firmly so it keeps even pressure on the chip, and its front and back vents set the path air takes through the box. Metal panels close to the main board also act as shields, keeping electrical noise in and grounding the board.
keyNumbers: About 36 cm long and 22 cm deep
Steel sheet typically around 1 mm thick
Holds parts adding up to about 3 kg
details.madeOf: Mostly pressed and folded steel sheet, sometimes with cast or moulded sections. Steel is stiff, cheap and blocks radio interference, which matters with so many fast signals on the board.

parts.name: Chassis frame

parts.description: Front button that turns the console on, puts it to sleep, or ejects a disc with a second button beside it.

details.didYouKnow: In rest mode the console is not really off: it can keep downloading updates and charging controllers through its USB ports while the screen is dark.
details.howItWorks: The button does not switch mains power directly. It sends a small low-voltage signal to a tiny always-on controller on the main board, which then starts the power supply, wakes the APU or puts the system into a low-power rest state. The eject button beside it works the same way, asking the disc drive to push the disc out.
keyNumbers: Fully off standby typically under about 1 W
Rest mode usually a few watts
Signal typically only a few volts
details.madeOf: A moulded plastic cap over a small switch or touch sensor on a circuit board behind the front panel. Plastic is cheap, light and easy to shape so the button sits flush with the case.

parts.name: Power button

parts.description: USB-C ports on the front for charging and connecting controllers.

details.didYouKnow: A USB-C plug has the same contacts on both sides, so it works either way up, ending the old ritual of flipping a USB plug over twice.
details.howItWorks: The front ports connect straight to USB controllers on the main board through a short flex cable or small daughter board. A controller plugged in here charges and can also talk to the console over the cable, which is handy for pairing a new controller. The ports can also carry data to external drives and accessories.
keyNumbers: USB-C connectors about 8.4 x 2.6 mm
Data speeds up to about 10 Gbps
Rated for roughly 10,000 plug-in cycles
details.madeOf: Stamped steel shells around plastic tongues carrying gold-plated copper contacts. The steel shell gives a strong, grounded housing, and gold plating resists corrosion so the contacts stay reliable.

parts.name: Front USB ports

parts.description: HDMI output for the TV, Ethernet, more USB and the power socket along the back.

details.didYouKnow: To reach 4K at 120 frames a second, the console must send the TV roughly a billion pixels every second, which is why a newer high-speed HDMI cable is needed.
details.howItWorks: The HDMI port carries the finished picture and sound to the TV, the Ethernet socket gives a wired network link, and USB ports connect drives and accessories. The power socket feeds mains electricity straight into the built-in power supply. Because the ports are soldered to the main board and poke through the chassis, the metal frame takes the strain when cables are pushed in.
keyNumbers: HDMI 2.1 output up to about 4K at 120 Hz
HDMI 2.1 bandwidth up to about 48 Gbps
Ethernet typically up to about 1 Gbps
details.madeOf: Stamped steel shells around plastic bodies with gold-plated copper contacts. The steel shells are grounded to the chassis to keep fast signals from leaking radio noise.

parts.name: Rear ports

parts.description: Large multi-layer circuit board that connects the chip, memory, storage, ports and power.

details.didYouKnow: Many of the wires on the board run inside it, in layers you can never see, and are linked by tiny drilled holes plated with copper called vias.
details.howItWorks: The main board is the console's road network: thousands of copper traces link the APU to its memory, storage, ports and power. Next to the APU, banks of voltage regulators take the 12 V from the power supply and step it down to around 1 V, delivering very large currents. Memory traces are carefully matched in length so signals arrive at exactly the right moment.
keyNumbers: Typically 8 or more copper layers
Chip core voltages roughly 1 V
Core currents can exceed about 100 A
details.madeOf: Layers of glass-fibre cloth soaked in epoxy resin, sandwiched with thin sheets of copper that are etched into wiring. Glass-fibre epoxy is strong, insulating and stable when it heats up.

parts.name: Main board

parts.description: Custom chip combining an eight-core processor and a powerful graphics unit on one piece of silicon.

details.didYouKnow: A teraflop is a trillion calculations a second, so the graphics unit does roughly ten trillion sums every second; the first home consoles had no programmable processor for graphics at all.
details.howItWorks: The APU puts a processor and a graphics unit on one piece of silicon. The processor runs the game's logic, physics and sound, while the graphics unit works out the colour of millions of pixels in parallel for every frame. Both share the same memory, so they can hand work to each other without copying it, and the chip constantly adjusts its speed to stay within its power and heat budget.
keyNumbers: 8 processor cores up to roughly 3.5 GHz
Graphics roughly 10 teraflops
Made on a roughly 6 to 7 nm class process
Die roughly 300 square millimetres
details.madeOf: Billions of transistors etched into a silicon die, mounted on a small fibreglass package with hundreds of solder connections underneath. The die sits face down so its back can touch the cooling layer directly.

parts.name: APU (processor & graphics)

parts.description: Ring of fast GDDR memory chips around the APU, shared by the processor and graphics.

details.didYouKnow: Earlier consoles often split memory into separate pools for the processor and graphics; sharing one fast pool lets developers decide for each game how much goes to each job.
details.howItWorks: The eight chips surround the APU in a ring so the wiring to each is short and nearly equal in length. Each chip has its own 32-bit connection, and together they form one wide 256-bit path that both the processor and graphics unit draw from. They hold textures, models and game data that need to be reached far faster than the SSD can manage, but lose everything when the power goes off.
keyNumbers: 8 chips of about 2 GB each, 16 GB total
Combined bandwidth roughly 448 GB/s
Each pin runs at about 14 Gbps
details.madeOf: Silicon memory dies packaged in black plastic with tiny solder balls underneath, soldered straight to the board. Soldering rather than using slots keeps connections short enough for very high speeds.

parts.name: Graphics memory chips

parts.description: Flash storage chips soldered to the board, read through a custom controller fast enough to stream game worlds on the fly.

details.didYouKnow: The spinning hard disks in earlier consoles read roughly 100 MB a second, so this SSD is around fifty times faster, which is why loading screens shrank from tens of seconds to a few.
details.howItWorks: Game data lives on several flash chips that a custom controller reads in parallel, like opening many taps at once. A built-in hardware decompressor unpacks the data as it streams in, so the processor does not have to. This is fast enough that games can load parts of the world just before you turn to look at them, instead of keeping everything in memory.
keyNumbers: About 825 GB to 1 TB of storage
Raw read speeds around 5.5 GB/s
Often around a dozen parallel channels
details.madeOf: Stacked NAND flash memory dies in plastic packages, soldered to the board around a controller chip. Flash keeps data without power and has no moving parts, so it is quick and silent.

parts.name: SSD storage chips

parts.description: Slot for an extra M.2 SSD to add more game storage, reached from under the top cover.

details.didYouKnow: The name M.2 refers to a card shape rather than a speed, so two drives that look identical can differ hugely in how fast they are.
details.howItWorks: An M.2 SSD stick slides into the slot at an angle and is held flat by a small screw at the far end. The slot connects to the APU over fast PCI Express lanes, and the console tests a new drive to check it is quick enough to run games from. Because fast drives get hot, a heat sink on the drive or a cover plate is used to keep it cool.
keyNumbers: M.2 cards typically 22 mm wide, 30 to 110 mm long
PCI Express 4.0 link up to roughly 8 GB/s
Recommended drives read at about 5.5 GB/s or faster
details.madeOf: A plastic connector with gold-plated spring contacts, soldered to the main board, with screw posts for different card lengths. Gold resists corrosion so the contacts stay reliable.

parts.name: Storage expansion slot

parts.description: Row of power stages and chokes that step the supply down to the roughly one volt, at very high current, the chip runs on.

details.didYouKnow: A faint buzzing from a console under load is often these coils: they vibrate very slightly as the current through them switches, which is called coil whine.
details.howItWorks: The power supply delivers a fairly high, steady voltage, but the chip wants about one volt at a very large current. Each phase here is a pair of fast transistors and a small coil that chop the input into pulses and smooth them out again; several phases take turns so no single one has to carry the whole load.
keyNumbers: Commonly several to a dozen or more phases
Output around 1 volt
Current can reach well over 100 amps at full load
details.madeOf: Power-stage chips, ferrite-cored inductors and polymer capacitors soldered to the main board, usually near the chip so the high current has only a short way to travel.

parts.name: Voltage regulators

parts.description: Large block of thin aluminium fins that air from the fan flows through, carrying away the APU's heat.

details.didYouKnow: Doubling the fin area roughly doubles how much heat the air can pick up, which is why console coolers pack in so many closely spaced fins rather than using one thick block of metal.
details.howItWorks: Heat from the APU enters through a solid base and is spread by heat pipes into hundreds of thin fins. The fins give a huge surface area so the air pushed through by the fan can pick up heat quickly before leaving through the rear vents. The memory chips and voltage regulators often get pads linking them to the same heat sink or to metal shields.
keyNumbers: Fins typically a fraction of a millimetre thick
Removes roughly 200 W while gaming
One of the heaviest single parts inside
details.madeOf: Thin stamped aluminium fins, with a copper or nickel-plated base where it meets the chip. Aluminium is light and cheap while conducting heat well, and copper at the base spreads heat even faster.

parts.name: Heat sink

parts.description: Sealed copper pipes that carry heat from the chip out across the whole heat sink.

details.didYouKnow: Heat pipes were developed in the 1960s for spacecraft, and they are a good reason this console can stay fairly quiet while getting rid of around 200 W.
details.howItWorks: Each pipe holds a little water under low pressure, so it boils at a low temperature. At the hot end over the chip, the water evaporates and the vapour rushes to the cooler fins, where it condenses and gives up its heat. A wick lining the inside then draws the liquid back to the hot end to repeat the cycle, with no pump at all.
keyNumbers: Typically about 6 to 8 mm across
Can move heat many times better than solid copper
Usually several pipes per cooler
details.madeOf: Copper tubes with a sintered copper powder or grooved wick inside, sealed with a small amount of water. Copper conducts heat very well and does not react with water.

parts.name: Heat pipes

parts.description: Thin layer of liquid metal between the APU and the heat sink that conducts heat far better than paste.

details.didYouKnow: Gallium eats into aluminium and makes it brittle, so the heat sink surface touching liquid metal has to be copper or nickel-plated rather than bare aluminium.
details.howItWorks: No two metal surfaces are perfectly flat, and tiny air gaps between the chip and the heat sink would trap heat. The liquid metal fills those gaps and carries heat across far better than ordinary paste. Because it conducts electricity and could short nearby parts if it escaped, it is held in place by a foam ring or seal around the chip.
keyNumbers: Layer typically a fraction of a millimetre thick
Conducts heat roughly several times better than paste
Spread over roughly 300 square millimetres of die
details.madeOf: A gallium-based alloy, often mixed with indium and tin, that stays liquid at room temperature. It conducts heat almost like a solid metal while still flowing into every gap.

parts.name: Liquid-metal thermal layer

parts.description: Ring around the fan that guides air in from the vents and pushes it through the heat sink.

details.didYouKnow: The spiral shape around a centrifugal fan is called a volute, the same idea used in water pumps and the snail-shaped casing of a car's turbocharger.
details.howItWorks: This is a centrifugal fan, so air is drawn in through the centre and flung outward by the spinning blades. The housing catches that air and, with its widening spiral shape, turns it into a steady stream aimed at the heat sink fins. It also keeps the air from looping straight back into the fan.
keyNumbers: Fan roughly 100 to 120 mm across
Fan about 45 mm thick
Can draw air in from both faces in some designs
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic, sometimes combined with parts of the metal frame. Plastic is light, quiet and easy to mould into the smooth curves that guide air without turbulence.

parts.name: Fan housing

parts.description: Blades of the large, slow-spinning fan that pulls cool air through the console.

details.didYouKnow: Fan noise climbs steeply with speed, so a big fan turning slowly is usually much quieter than a small fan spinning fast to move the same air.
details.howItWorks: The 32 curved blades sweep air outward as the wheel spins, pulling fresh air in through the centre to take its place. Having many blades lets the fan move plenty of air while turning slowly, which keeps the sound low and less whiny. Their shape and spacing are tuned to reduce the tone caused by each blade passing the housing.
keyNumbers: 32 blades on one wheel
Wheel roughly 100 to 120 mm across
Fan about 45 mm thick
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic, often reinforced with glass fibre, formed in one piece with the hub. Plastic is light, so the wheel spins up quickly and stays balanced with little effort.

parts.name: Fan blades

parts.description: Brushless motor in the hub of the fan, sped up and slowed down to match how hot the chip is running.

details.didYouKnow: Consoles like this can have their fan behaviour changed after release through software updates, tuning how hard it spins based on real-world temperatures.
details.howItWorks: Electromagnets in the fixed centre are switched on and off in turn by a small circuit, pulling a ring of magnets inside the spinning hub round and round. Temperature sensors on the main board and the APU tell the system how hot things are, and it sends a speed signal to the motor. Because there are no brushes rubbing, it can run quietly for years.
keyNumbers: Runs on about 12 V
Drives a fan wheel roughly 100 to 120 mm across
Typically rated for tens of thousands of hours
details.madeOf: Copper wire coils on a steel core, permanent magnets in the hub and a small control chip, inside a plastic hub. The brushless design avoids wear and sparks.

parts.name: Fan motor

parts.description: Moulded duct that catches the air thrown out of the side of the fan and spreads it across the front of the heat sink.

details.didYouKnow: Much of what you hear from a console is air turbulence rather than the motor, so careful duct shapes can make it quieter without changing the fan at all.
details.howItWorks: A centrifugal fan flings air out sideways rather than along its axis. This moulded duct catches that sideways stream, turns the corner and spreads it evenly across the front of the fin stack, so all the fins get air and little of it leaks around them.
keyNumbers: Usually just a few millimetres of wall thickness
Runs roughly the full height of the fin stack
Gaps of even a millimetre or two can leak noticeable air
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic with thin foam or rubber seals where it meets the heat sink. Plastic is light, cheap, and easy to shape into the smooth curves that keep the airflow quiet.

parts.name: Air duct

parts.description: Built-in power supply that turns mains electricity into the steady low voltage the chips need.

details.didYouKnow: Building the power supply inside, rather than using a bulky power brick, means a single plain mains cable is all the console needs.
details.howItWorks: Mains electricity first goes through filters, is turned into direct current, then is switched on and off tens of thousands of times a second or more through a small transformer. This switching design steps the voltage down to around 12 V far more efficiently than an old heavy transformer could. Voltage regulators on the main board then trim it further to what each chip needs.
keyNumbers: Rated roughly 300 to 350 W
Works on about 100 to 240 V mains
Main output about 12 V
Typically roughly 85 to 90 percent efficient
details.madeOf: Capacitors, coils, transistors and a transformer on a circuit board inside a vented metal shield. The metal shield blocks electrical noise and keeps mains voltage safely enclosed.

parts.name: Power supply

parts.description: Slot-loading Blu-ray drive that reads game and film discs with a blue-violet laser.

details.didYouKnow: The format is spelt Blu-ray without an e because an everyday phrase like blue ray could not be registered as a trademark.
details.howItWorks: Rollers draw the disc in and clamp it onto a motor that spins it. A laser focused through a lens shines on the disc's spiral track, and tiny pits and flat areas reflect the light differently, which a sensor reads as data. Because a disc is much slower than the SSD, games are copied onto internal storage before you play.
keyNumbers: Blue-violet laser about 405 nm
Discs hold up to about 100 GB
Track spacing about 0.32 micrometres
details.madeOf: A metal frame with a spindle motor, a moving laser head with a small lens, and plastic guides and rollers. Metal keeps the mechanism stiff so the laser stays precisely aligned.

parts.name: Blu-ray disc drive

parts.description: Sled carrying the laser and lens, walked along steel rails beneath the disc from its centre to its edge as the disc spins on the motor.

details.didYouKnow: Blue-violet light has a shorter wavelength than the red used in DVD players, so it focuses to a smaller spot. That is what lets a disc of the same size hold several times as much.
details.howItWorks: A blue-violet laser shines up through the lens and focuses to a tiny spot on the spinning disc's data layer. Pits and flat areas reflect differently, and a sensor reads that as ones and zeros. The lens is hung on tiny coils that keep it in focus as the disc wobbles, while the whole sled is walked out along its rails by a small motor and lead screw.
keyNumbers: Laser wavelength of about 405 nanometres
A single layer holds about 25 GB
Disc is 120 mm across
details.madeOf: A plastic and metal sled carrying a laser diode, a light sensor, small mirrors and a lens on a magnetic suspension, running on polished steel rails. A flat flexible cable lets it move.

parts.name: Laser pickup

summary: A modern home games console: a custom chip that combines a PC-class processor and graphics, fast memory and storage, a big fan and heat sink to cool it, a built-in power supply and a disc drive, inside a plastic shell.
